To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the generalization performance of stochastic gradient methods is determined by the stability and approximation errors, (2) both the stability and approximation error can be controlled by either the step-size (when the number of passes is fixed) or the number of the passes (when the step size is fixed), (3) the step-size and the number of passes can be seen to implicitly regularize the solution.

(i) the stability of the algorithm can, in principle, be tuned by the choice of the number of passes; (ii) the stability can be tuned in practice by the choice of step-size and number of passes; and (iii) the number of passes can be tuned in a way that is consistent with implicit regularization.
the number of passes can be used to control implicit regularization and that this can lead to better generalization.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number of passes is the most relevant tuning parameter in SGM for generalization.
, for the case of convex losses, stochastic gradient methods can achieve the best generalization properties when the number of passes is set to the optimal value.

, in the case of convex losses and linearly parameterizable functions, the generalization properties and implicit regularization can be controlled by the number of passes and step-size.
